props.title: Luck and Risk
lines: Luck and risk are the same coin. We see the winner and ignore the roommate who died.
Judge processes, not one outcome. Nothing is as good or as bad as it looks.

props.title: Bill Gates, Paul Allen, Kent Evans

left.name: The lucky room
lines: Lakeside had a computer when almost no high school did — Gates and Allen used it.
1968: roughly 303 million high-school-age people in the world; about 18 million in the U.S.
Start with 303 million, end with a few hundred in that building. That is luck.

right.name: The missing partner
lines: Kent Evans was Gates's best friend and classmate in that same room.
He died in a mountaineering accident as a teenager.
Same unusual environment: one path to Microsoft, one funeral. Luck and risk arrived together.

rows.v: Yahoo offered about $1 billion to buy Facebook. Mark Zuckerberg said no.
Because Facebook later became enormous, the refusal is taught as genius.
If Facebook had stalled, the same no would be taught as arrogance.
Risk is what remains after you subtract luck from a good outcome. Do not copy leverage from a winner's highlight reel.

props.kicker: WHAT TO DO WITH LUCK AND RISK
props.title: The chapter's working rules
items: Do not assume a rich person is purely skilled, or a broke person is purely foolish.
Look at decisions under their control, then at timing, health, and one-off breaks.
The book's line: nothing is as good or as bad as it looks.
That humility stops you cloning someone else's debt, and quitting a good process after one bad year.

rows.v: Gates and Allen turned a rare high-school computer into a company. That is skill plus a door that almost nobody else had.
Kent Evans sat at the same table and never got the second act. Risk is luck's twin, not its opposite.
Be slower to praise winners as geniuses and slower to damn losers as fools.
Copying a winner's leverage copies their unseen risk, not just their return.

props.title: Hold skill loosely
items: Bill Gates got a computer. Kent Evans sat at the same table and did not get a second act.
Yahoo's Facebook offer is genius or arrogance depending on a future nobody knew in two thousand six.
When you copy a winner, you may be copying an unseen accident, not a method.
The book's line again: nothing is as good or as bad as it looks.
